Read the Bible Monday to Friday and keep the weekend for rest, catching up or deeper reflection.
Each day contains a balanced portion from the Old Testament and exactly one chapter from the New Testament.
Introduction to The Balanced Plan ({0} days a week)
This plan offers a structured and sustainable path through the whole Bible in one year, with a daily balance between the Old and New Testaments and room for rest and reflection at the weekends.
The Balanced Plan is designed to make Bible reading a natural part of your everyday life without overwhelming you.
By reading five days a week you get a steady flow of God's Word, while the weekends give you freedom to go deeper, catch up on missed days or simply rest in what you have learned.
Each reading day combines deep insight from the Old Testament with a chapter from the New Testament, giving you a full picture of God's plan of salvation.
God's story of salvation

The plan follows the unfolding of God's covenant with humanity, from creation and the fall, through the history of Israel, to the coming of Jesus Christ and the growth of the church, showing the common thread in God's plan of salvation.
The balance between law and grace

By reading from both the Old and New Testaments every day, you will discover how God's righteousness and holiness in the law find their fulfilment in the grace and salvation offered through Jesus Christ, and how the two complete each other.
Practical discipleship

The daily readings, especially from the New Testament, give guidance for Christian living, ethics and building the church, and challenge you to apply God's Word in everyday life and grow in faith and practice.

Romans: The Foundation of Faith
Paul's letter to the Romans is the most systematic presentation of the Christian message and God's plan of salvation.
A demanding but deeply rewarding {0}-day journey.
Introduction to Romans: The Foundation of Faith
Romans reveals God's righteousness and plan of salvation through faith in Jesus Christ, and lays an unshakable foundation for Christian faith and life.
Welcome to a {0}-day journey through Romans, Paul's most systematic and profound presentation of the Christian message.
This letter is a cornerstone of theology that carefully explains God's plan of salvation for humanity.
Get ready for a demanding but deeply rewarding study that will strengthen your understanding of the foundation of faith.
God's righteousness and human sin
The letter shows the universal sin that separates people from God, and presents God's righteousness as the only way to reconciliation.
Justification by faith
Paul explains how people are declared righteous before God, not through works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ alone.
Life in the Spirit and sanctification
Explore how believers are set free from the power of sin and called to a new life led by the Holy Spirit, marked by holiness and freedom.
Human sin and God's salvation
This section shows the universal reach of sin and the role of the law, and presents God's solution: justification by faith alone.
Freedom from sin and new life in the Spirit
Here we explore what justification brings – freedom from the power of sin and the victorious life led by the Holy Spirit.
God's faithfulness and the mystery of salvation
Paul addresses God's unchanging plan for Israel and the Gentiles, and shows how God keeps his promises.
Practical Christian living and fellowship
The final chapters give guidance for a holy life, serving in the church, our relationship to the authorities and love in the fellowship.
Day {0}: The Gospel as the Power of God
Romans opens with a powerful declaration of the nature and power of the gospel.
Paul introduces himself as a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle to proclaim God's gospel about his Son.
He declares: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel.
It is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes."
He goes on to reveal the condition of humanity without God – where we have exchanged God's truth for a lie and worshipped the creation rather than the Creator.
This chapter challenges us to see the unique place of the gospel in our world.
It is not just a philosophy or a moral system, but God's own dynamic power to transform lives.

When we see the confusion and darkness in the society around us, we are called to stand firm and bold on the truth of the gospel, knowing that it brings the light and salvation people desperately need.
Pray/Reflect: Lord Jesus, thank you that the gospel is your living power in my life.
Give me boldness never to be ashamed of your Word, but to share it in love.
Day {0}: God's Righteous Judgement and the Condition of the Heart
In {R0} chapter {0}, Paul turns his attention to the religious and self-righteous who judge others.
He reminds us that God's judgement is true and impartial.
Knowing God's law or bearing outward religious signs is worthless if the heart is not transformed.
"A person is not a Jew who is one outwardly...
true circumcision is circumcision of the heart, by the Spirit and not by the letter."
Paul warns us against the trap of feeling superior to others because we know the Bible.
God's kindness is meant to lead us to repentance, not to pride.
What God is looking for is a sincere and humble heart shaped by the Holy Spirit.
Let us examine our own motives and ask God for a pure heart marked by genuine grace and love.
Pray/Reflect: Dear God, search my heart and cleanse me from all self-righteousness.
Let your kindness lead me to daily repentance and honesty before you.
Day {0}: Justified Freely by Grace
{R0} contains one of the absolute theological high points of the Bible.
Paul concludes that "all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God".
No one can become righteous before God by their own works or by keeping the law.

But right in this darkness the light of the gospel shines: we are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God put forward as an atoning sacrifice through faith in his blood.
This is the heart of our Christian faith.
Our righteousness is not built on our achievements, but on Jesus' finished work on the cross.
When the enemy accuses us of our failures, we can rest in the complete assurance that God has declared us righteous in Christ.
Faith receives what grace offers as a free gift.
Pray/Reflect: Thank you, Lord Jesus, that your sacrifice on the cross gave me complete freedom and righteousness.
I receive your undeserved grace with thankfulness.
Day {0}: Abraham's Faith as a Pattern
In {R0} chapter {0}, Paul uses Abraham as the perfect example of justification by faith.
Abraham was not declared righteous because he was circumcised or kept the law – this happened long before the law was given!
"Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness."
Against all hope he believed, fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.
Abraham's faith is an example for us today.
Faith is not seeing the solution with natural eyes, but fixing our eyes on God's unshakable promises even when circumstances look impossible.
When we put our trust in the God who gives life to the dead and calls into being things that were not, our faith is credited to us as righteousness.
Pray/Reflect: Father, strengthen my faith so I can hold on to your promises even in hardship.
Thank you that my faith in Jesus makes me an heir of your blessings.
Day {0}: Peace with God and the Abundance of Grace
{R0} paints a wonderful picture of the fruit of our justification.
"Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ."

We even glory in our sufferings, because suffering produces perseverance, perseverance produces character, and character produces hope – a hope that does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit.
Paul compares Adam and Christ: while sin brought death through one man, grace brings abundant life through one man, Jesus Christ.
This chapter gives us a deep, unshakable inner peace.
We are no longer God's enemies, but his beloved children standing firmly in grace.
Whatever storms we face in everyday life, God's grace is always greater than the power of sin and painful circumstances.
Pray/Reflect: Dear Father, thank you for the peace you have given me.
Thank you that your love fills my heart and that your grace is always more than enough for me.
Day {0}: Dead to Sin, Alive to God
In {R0}, Paul raises the burning question: Shall we go on sinning so that grace may increase?
The answer is a firm no!
Through baptism we were buried with Christ into death, so that just as Christ was raised from the dead, we too may live a new life.
Our old self was crucified with him, so that we should no longer be slaves to sin.
This is a fundamental truth about the identity of the believer.
We do not fight sin in order to be accepted; we live victoriously because we are already dead to the rule of sin and alive to God in Christ.
Paul urges us to offer every part of ourselves to God as instruments of righteousness.
Pray/Reflect: Lord, thank you that sin no longer has power over me.
I give you my body, my thoughts and my words today as instruments of your righteousness.
Day {0}: The Struggle in Our Own Strength
{R0} chapter {0} describes the inner conflict that arises when a person tries to keep God's holy law in their own human strength.
Paul puts words to the familiar pain: "For I do not do the good I want to do.
But the evil I do not want to do – this I keep on doing."
The law itself is good and holy, but it has no power to transform our human nature – it only exposes our weakness.
The chapter reaches its low point with the cry: "What a wretched man I am!
Who will rescue me from this body that is subject to death?"
But the answer comes at once with a shout of thanks: "Thanks be to God, who delivers me through Jesus Christ our Lord!"
{R0} shows us that it is impossible to live the Christian life by our own performance, and prepares us for the wonderful freedom of life in the Spirit in chapter {0}.
Pray/Reflect: Father, forgive me when I try to live in my own strength.
Thank you that you set me free from legalism and self-effort through Jesus Christ.
Day {0}: Life in the Spirit and God's Unconquerable Love
Many consider {R0} the most beautiful and powerful chapter in the Bible.
It begins with the monumental truth: "Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus."
Those who are led by God's Spirit are God's children, who can cry "Abba, Father!".
The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are God's children and co-heirs with Christ.
The chapter reaches its peak with the promise that nothing – neither hardship, persecution, powers nor the future – can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus!
When we live in the Spirit, we have not received a spirit of slavery that makes us afraid, but the Spirit of adoption.
Even when we do not know what to pray for, the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groans that words cannot express.
We are more than conquerors through him who loved us!
Pray/Reflect: Dear Abba Father, thank you that there is never again any condemnation for me.
Thank you that nothing in the whole universe can separate me from your unconquerable love.
Day {0}: God's Choice and Sovereignty
In {R0} chapter {0}, Paul expresses his deepest sorrow for his own people, Israel, who have largely rejected their Messiah.
He dives into the theology of God's sovereign choice and mercy.
God is like the potter who has the right to shape the clay as he wishes.
God's promises to Israel have not failed, for it is not the children by physical descent who are God's children, but the children of the promise.
This chapter calls us to deep humility before God's greatness and sovereignty.
We cannot hold God to account or demand anything on the basis of our own merits.
Everything rests on his mercy.
It also challenges us to carry a burning burden for the people around us and for God's own people to come to know Jesus.
Pray/Reflect: Heavenly Father, I bow before your sovereign wisdom and goodness.
Give me your love and a burning burden for those who do not yet know your Son.
Day {0}: Faith in the Heart and Confession with the Mouth
{R0} is about how a person receives salvation.
Paul stresses that Christ is the culmination of the law, so that there may be righteousness for everyone who believes.
Salvation is not out of reach or far away; "The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart".
If you declare with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.
And Paul asks boldly: "How can they believe in the one of whom they have not heard?
And how can they hear without someone preaching to them?"
This is the heart of mission and of personal faith.
Salvation is available to everyone who calls on the name of the Lord.
We are all called to carry this good news out, for faith comes from hearing the message, and the message is heard through the word about Christ.
Pray/Reflect: Lord Jesus, you are my Lord and Saviour.
Use my mouth to boldly confess your truth and share your gospel with the people I meet.
Day {0}: God's Faithfulness to Israel and the Depth of Grace
In {R0}, Paul assures us that God has not rejected his people Israel.
There is always a remnant chosen by grace.
He uses the picture of a cultivated olive tree, into which the Gentiles have been grafted as wild branches.
Paul warns believers from a Gentile background against being proud, for it is the root that supports the branches, not the other way round.
Finally Paul bursts into a wonderful song of praise to God's unsearchable wisdom.
God's faithfulness to Israel is the guarantee that he is also faithful to his promises to you and me.
If God could break his oldest promises, we could never trust the blessings of the New Testament.
But God is unchangingly faithful!
He weaves his story together for the salvation of the whole world.
Pray/Reflect: "Oh, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!"
Thank you for your unshakable faithfulness.
I trust in your eternal promises.
Day {0}: Living Sacrifice and Practical Love
{R0} marks the move from deep theology to practical Christian living.
In view of God's mercy, Paul urges us to offer our bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God.
We are not to conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of our minds.
The chapter is full of practical encouragement to serve with the gifts we have received, to love sincerely, to bless those who persecute us and to overcome evil with good.
Worship is not just something we do on Sundays, but the way we live every single day.
When our minds are renewed by God's Word, we learn to test and approve what God's will is – his good, pleasing and perfect will.
Genuine faith shows itself in practical kindness, trust and love in the fellowship.
Pray/Reflect: Lord, I give you my body and my mind today.
Renew my thoughts so I can live a life that honours you and overcomes evil with good.
Day {0}: Authorities, the Command to Love and the Armour of Light
{R0} deals with believers' relationship to society and the authorities, which are established by God to keep order and protect what is good.
Paul stresses that love is the fulfilment of the law – to owe no one anything except to love one another.
He then sounds a wake-up call: The night is nearly over, the day is almost here!
So let us put aside the deeds of darkness and put on the armour of light and the Lord Jesus Christ.
As believers we are called to be model citizens who show respect, pay taxes and promote peace, while our highest loyalty belongs to God.
We live in the light of Jesus' soon return, which calls us to wake up from spiritual sleep and live a pure, shining life clothed with Christ.
Pray/Reflect: Lord Jesus, clothe me with your armour of light today.
Help me fulfil the command to love in my meetings with all people and to live as a child of the day.
Day {0}: Room for Differences and Building Each Other Up
In {R0} chapter {0}, Paul deals with disagreements on secondary questions, such as food rules and holy days.
He urges believers to accept those who are weak in faith without judging or looking down on each other.
"For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit."
We should make every effort to do what leads to peace and to building each other up.
This chapter gives deep wisdom for Christian fellowship.
We must never let personal opinions or freedoms become a stumbling block for other believers.
Our burning desire should be to build up our brothers and sisters and keep the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace.
Pray/Reflect: Father, give me a generous heart that does not judge others.
Let me seek what builds up my neighbour and promotes your peace and joy in the fellowship.
Day {0}: Christ's Example and the Vision for Mission
{R0} urges the strong to bear with the failings of the weak and not to please themselves, just as Christ did not please himself.
Paul prays that the God of hope will fill us with all joy and peace as we trust in him, so that we may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.
He also shares his burning vision to preach the gospel where Christ's name is not yet known.
Paul reminds us that the goal of all sound theology is a life of worship, mission and care for one another.
When we are filled with the power of the Holy Spirit, our lives overflow with a living hope that we long to share with unreached places and the people around us.
Pray/Reflect: "God of hope, fill me with all joy and peace as I trust in you, so that I may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit!"
Day {0}: Personal Greetings and Eternal Praise
Romans ends in chapter {0} with a warm series of personal greetings to more than thirty named co-workers in Rome – women and men, slaves and free, leaders and servants.
Paul mentions Phoebe, Priscilla, Aquila and many others who have risked their lives for the gospel.
The letter closes with a magnificent doxology that praises the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, for ever!
This ending shows that God's kingdom is built through close, faithful relationships and working together.
No servant is unimportant in God's eyes.
When we stand together in faith and love, the God of peace will soon crush Satan under our feet.
To him be the glory for ever!
Pray/Reflect: To him who is able to establish you...
to the only wise God be glory for ever through Jesus Christ!
The Gospel of John: Who Is Jesus?
The ultimate recommendation for anyone who wants to get to know Jesus better.
Go deeper into Jesus' unique words, signs and "I am" sayings over {0} days.
Introduction to the Gospel of John
The Gospel of John was written so that we may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and that by believing we may have life in his name.
The Gospel of John gives us a unique picture of who Jesus is.

While the other three Gospels (the Synoptics) focus much on Jesus' deeds and parables in Galilee, John takes us on a deeper theological journey to reveal Jesus' divine nature and his close relationship with the Father.
The Word became flesh
Jesus is the eternal Logos who was with God and was God.
The seven signs
Selected miracles that reveal Jesus' glory and awaken faith.
The "I am" sayings
Seven times Jesus reveals his identity using God's own covenant name (for example, the Bread of Life and the Light of the World).
The prologue
The true light comes into the world.
The Book of Signs
Jesus' public ministry.
The Book of Glory
The farewell discourse, the cross and the resurrection.

The epilogue
Breakfast by the lake and the restoration of Peter.
Chapter {0}: The Light That Overcomes the Darkness
The Gospel of John opens with one of the most monumental declarations in the Bible: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."
This is not just a historical starting point, but an eternal truth about Jesus Christ.
He is the Word (Logos), the pre-existent, divine Creator through whom all things were made.
He is the source of life and the light of humanity, a light that no darkness can overcome.
This chapter lifts the veil on Jesus' true identity – not just a prophet or a good man, but God himself, come to earth.
The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us, full of grace and truth.
This incarnation is the heart of the gospel, where the invisible God became visible, touchable and relatable in Jesus.
What does this mean for us today?
The Gospel of John invites us to receive this light, to believe in his name and so receive the right to become children of God.
In a world marked by uncertainty and darkness, Jesus is our unchanging anchor and guiding star.
To "receive" him is about more than intellectual agreement; it is actively surrendering our lives to him who is the truth and the life.
It means letting his light expose our shadows, guide our steps and fill us with the grace and truth found only in him.
Today, let us choose to walk in his light, let his divine presence transform our thoughts, words and actions, and reflect his glory to the world around us.
Pray/Reflect: Lord Jesus, thank you that you are the Word, the light and the life.
Help me receive you fully today and walk in your truth.
The Bible Project: The Gospel of John {0}-{1}
Chapter {0}: Jesus' Glory and the New Reality
John chapter {0} presents two striking events that powerfully reveal who Jesus is.
At the wedding in Cana we see Jesus show his divine power and glory for the first time by turning water into excellent wine.
This is not just a miracle; it is a sign pointing to his identity as the true bridegroom, the one who brings abundance, joy and the "best wine" – the new life and the new covenant in him.
What he does shows compassion and the ability to fill our lack and go beyond our expectations.
Shortly afterwards he cleanses the temple, an act that shows his burning zeal for God's house and his authority over religious systems.
He also points to a deeper truth: that his own body is the new temple, which will be destroyed and raised again – a prophecy of his death and resurrection.
Both events proclaim Jesus' unique divinity and his role as the one who begins a completely new reality.
The wedding in Cana reminds us that Jesus can turn the ordinary into the extraordinary in our lives.
Just as he transformed water, he can transform our disappointments, our lack and our everyday routines into something filled with his abundance and joy.
He invites us to bring our "empty jars" to him and trust that he will fill them in a way that goes beyond anything we can imagine.
The cleansing of the temple challenges us to examine our own "temples" – our hearts and lives.
Have we let worldly things or self-interest take the place that belongs to God?
Jesus calls us to purity and wholehearted devotion to him.
As his disciples, let us "do whatever he tells us", and experience his transforming power and the new reality he offers in every part of our lives.
Pray/Reflect: Lord Jesus, thank you that you are the one who transforms and cleanses.
Help me give my "empty jars" to you and let you cleanse my heart, so that I can live a life that honours you and experience your abundance.
Chapter {0}: God's Boundless Love and the New Life
John chapter {0} invites us into a deep encounter between Jesus and Nicodemus, a leading Pharisee.
Nicodemus, a man of the law and tradition, came to Jesus under cover of night, and there Jesus revealed a fundamental truth: "No one can see the kingdom of God unless they are born again."
This is not a physical rebirth, but a spiritual transformation, a work of the Holy Spirit.
It is about receiving new life from God, a life that changes our perspective and our direction.
Jesus stresses here that salvation is not based on human achievement or religious background, but on God's sovereign action and our faith in him.

The climax of this message is the eternal truth of {R0}, which reveals God's unimaginable love for the world, shown in that he gave his one and only Son, so that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life.
Jesus is the only way to this new life.
For us today the message is just as relevant.
It reminds us that our spiritual life is not something we can earn, but a gift we receive by faith.
Every day is an opportunity to live out this new life, led by the Spirit and rooted in God's love.
It means surrendering to Jesus, recognising our dependence on him and letting his character be formed in us.
As John the Baptist testified: "He must become greater; I must become less."
This is a call to humility, to give Jesus more room in our lives, our thoughts and our actions.
In practice it means making time for God's Word a priority, seeking fellowship with other believers and letting our gratitude for salvation shine out to the world around us.
Let us embrace the radical truth that we are loved and renewed by God, and live accordingly.
Pray/Reflect: Lord, thank you for the new life you have given me through faith in Jesus.
Help me let you grow in me every day.
Chapter {0}: The Meeting at the Well: Living Water for All
{R0} paints a moving picture of Jesus' radical love and divine insight.
At Jacob's well we meet Jesus deliberately breaking down every social, religious and ethnic barrier.
He begins a deep conversation with a Samaritan woman – something unthinkable for a Jewish rabbi at the time.
In this conversation Jesus reveals himself not just as a prophet, but as the Messiah, the Christ, the one who gives "living water".
This water is more than something that quenches thirst; it is eternal life, a spring that never runs dry, a Spirit who renews and fills us from within.
It is an invitation to true worship, "in the Spirit and in truth", which goes beyond outward forms and rituals.
Jesus looks past the woman's past and status; he sees her heart and offers her the most precious thing – himself.
{R0} reminds us that Jesus still sees us, whatever our background, our mistakes or our doubts.
He comes to us with the living water that satisfies our deepest thirst for meaning, peace and belonging.
Our task is to receive this water and let it flow out from us to others.
Just as the Samaritan woman became an evangelist to her town, we are called to share the message about Jesus with the people around us.
Let us break down our own inner barriers and prejudices, and see people with Jesus' eyes – as individuals longing for truth and life.
Be willing to start conversations, show radical love and point to Jesus as the only source of eternal life.
Reflect: Who in your life needs to hear about the living water, and how can you be a bridge to Jesus this week?
Chapter {0}: Jesus' Divine Authority and Life-Giving Power
John chapter {0} reveals Jesus not just as a healer, but as the very source of life and authority, equal to God the Father.
At the pool of Bethesda he heals a man who has been ill for {0} years, and breaks the Sabbath rules of the day by telling him to carry his mat.
This sparks a deep theological debate in which Jesus explains his divine identity: "My Father is always at his work to this very day, and I too am working."
He claims full equality with the Father in work, honour and power, and says that the Father has given him authority to give life and to judge.
Jesus is not just a messenger, but the Son of God who exercises the Father's own authority, and he is the only way to know and honour God.
His actions testify to a power beyond the human, a power to raise the dead and give eternal life to whoever hears his word.
This truth about Jesus' divine authority is deeply relevant for us today.
Like the man by the pool, we can feel paralysed by circumstances, sin or a lack of hope.
But Jesus, who has power over time and illness, is ready to give us new life – both spiritually and physically.
Our challenge is to acknowledge his authority and trust him as the source of everything.
Perhaps, like the religious leaders, we let human honour or traditions overshadow the clear truth about who Jesus is.
Let us search the Scriptures, which testify about him, and let his word awaken us to a life of faith and obedience.
To honour the Son is to honour the Father, and in this lies our true freedom and peace.
Pray/Reflect: Lord Jesus, I acknowledge your divine authority over my life.
Help me always to seek honour from you, and to trust you as the source of eternal life.
Chapter {0}: The Bread of Life from Heaven
{R0} is a chapter that challenges how we understand our needs and what satisfies us.
After miraculously feeding five thousand people with bread and fish, Jesus confronts the crowd with a deeper truth: the physical food they are looking for only satisfies for a while.
Jesus presents himself as "the Bread of Life" – the true food that gives eternal life.
He is not just someone who
gives
bread; he
is
the very bread from heaven, sent by the Father to give life to the world.

This is a radical claim that lifts Jesus far beyond an earthly teacher or miracle worker; he is the divine source of all spiritual and eternal life, the only one who can satisfy the deepest hunger and thirst of our souls.
What does it mean to "eat" this bread today?
It means coming to Jesus in faith again and again, letting his words be our daily food, and letting his sacrifice on the cross be the foundation of our lives.
In a world that constantly tempts us with passing pleasures and shallow answers to our inner emptiness, Jesus calls us to a deeper and more lasting satisfaction.
Our spiritual hunger cannot be satisfied by success, possessions or human approval.
Only Jesus, the Bread of Life, can fill that emptiness.
Let us actively seek him every day, let his truth shape our thoughts and actions, and trust that he will satisfy us with a life that never ends.
Pray/Reflect: Lord Jesus, you are the Bread of Life.
Help me come to you every day to be satisfied, so that I will never again hunger for what does not last.
Chapter {0}: The Source of Living Water
{R0} presents an intense drama during the Festival of Tabernacles, where the tension around Jesus reaches its peak.
In the middle of the crowd's confusion, his brothers' scepticism and the hostility of the authorities, Jesus stands with unshakable authority.
He does not teach from human wisdom, but declares that his teaching comes from God himself – the one who sent him.
This chapter underlines Jesus' unique position as the one sent by God, whose time and mission are set by the Father.
He is not just a prophet or teacher, but the truth in person, revealing God's heart and plan, even when his identity causes division and debate.

From the very first second God identifies with the simple, the humble and the overlooked.
Wherever you are in life today, the Lord remembers you and meets you where you are.
The Sermon on the Mount
Jesus' words in the Sermon on the Mount turn every human standard of power and success upside down.
He calls the poor in spirit, those who mourn and those who thirst for righteousness 'blessed' (happy and favoured).

Let Jesus' words sink deep into your heart – it takes strength to be gentle, and God strengthens you.

We can call the Lord of all things our Dad!
Jesus also reminds us of the lilies of the field and the birds of the air.

You are never alone either when the storms or desert seasons of life rage.

Open your heart and let the Word put down deep roots so it can bear fruitful faith.

Practical Living
Trust in the Lord
Trust in the Lord with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding!
In all your ways submit to him, and he will make your paths straight.
Human logic only goes so far, and it often leads to needless dead ends and worries.
Wisdom begins by recognising that God knows best, and placing all our choices and plans in his mighty hands every morning.
Guard your heart
Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it!
The thoughts, words and impressions we let into our minds and hearts will in the end colour and shape our whole life.
Protect your heart from bitterness, anger and harmful influences.
Fill it instead with good words, wisdom, grace and trust, and good fruit will grow in every area of life.
The Lord directs our steps
In their hearts humans plan their course, but the Lord establishes their steps.

Trust his perfect timing and loving care today.
Doers of the word, not just hearers
Do not merely listen to the word, and so deceive yourselves. Do what it says!
James challenges us to a practical, concrete faith.

Let your faith be seen through your love today.

God opposes the proud but shows favour to the humble.
James asks us to humble ourselves under God's mighty hand and come near to him.

Sabiduría para la vida
Siete días de sabiduría sana para la vida, principios éticos y consejos espirituales prácticos de Salomón y del apóstol Santiago.
Vida práctica
Confía en el Señor
¡Confía en el Señor con todo tu corazón y no te apoyes en tu propia prudencia!
Reconócelo en todos tus caminos, y él enderezará tus sendas.
La lógica humana solo llega hasta cierto punto, y a menudo nos lleva a callejones sin salida y a preocupaciones innecesarias.
La sabiduría comienza reconociendo que Dios sabe más, y poniendo cada mañana todas nuestras decisiones y planes en sus manos poderosas.
Guarda tu corazón
¡Sobre todas las cosas guarda tu corazón, porque de él mana la vida!
Los pensamientos, las palabras y las impresiones que dejamos entrar en la mente y el corazón terminarán dando color y forma a toda nuestra vida.
Protege tu corazón de la amargura, la ira y las influencias dañinas.
Llénalo en cambio de buenas palabras, sabiduría, gracia y confianza, y crecerán buenos frutos en todas las áreas de tu vida.
El Señor dirige nuestros pasos
El corazón del hombre traza su camino, pero el Señor dirige sus pasos.
Es bueno y natural hacer planes y tener ambiciones, pero siempre debemos sostenerlos con la mano abierta.
A veces Dios cierra puertas para protegernos o para llevarnos a un camino aún mejor que todavía no podemos ver.
Confía hoy en su tiempo perfecto y en su cuidado amoroso.
Hacedores de la palabra, no solo oidores
¡Sed hacedores de la palabra y no tan solo oidores, engañándoos a vosotros mismos!
Santiago nos desafía a una fe práctica y concreta.
La fe no es solo teología correcta o palabras bonitas un domingo: es ayudar a los necesitados, guardarse de la dureza del mundo y dejar que la Palabra de Dios transforme nuestras acciones cada día.
Que tu fe se vea hoy a través de tu amor.
El poder de la lengua
La lengua es una parte pequeña del cuerpo, pero puede hacer mucho daño, como una chispa pequeña que incendia todo un bosque.
Santiago nos recuerda el gran poder de nuestras palabras.
Podemos usar la boca para bendecir y alabar a nuestro Padre celestial, pero también para herir a personas creadas a imagen de Dios.
Pide a Dios que guarde tu boca hoy, y en cambio comparte palabras de ánimo, edificación y vida con las personas que encuentres.
Humildad ante todo
Dios resiste a los soberbios y da gracia a los humildes.
Santiago nos pide que nos humillemos bajo la poderosa mano de Dios y nos acerquemos a él.
La promesa es maravillosa: ¡entonces él se acercará a nosotros!
La humildad no significa pensar mal de uno mismo, sino pensar menos en uno mismo y confiar más en Dios.
Busca su rostro en oración hoy, y él te levantará.
Perseverancia y oración eficaz
La oración del justo, obrando eficazmente, puede mucho.
Terminamos este viaje de sabiduría con el rico recordatorio de Santiago sobre el poder de la oración en tiempos de enfermedad y prueba.
Señala al profeta Elías, que era un ser humano común como nosotros, pero que oró con fe y vio grandes maravillas de Dios.
No abandones la oración: tu oración llega hasta el trono del cielo y obra milagros.
